title: Google Adds Cycle-Level Kernel Profiling to XProf
gist: Google added a Kernel Profiling suite to its open-source XProf TPU profiler, giving cycle-level visibility into custom Pallas/Mosaic/Triton kernels on TPU v7 (Ironwood) that previously appeared as opaque blocks, exemplified by a demo where identifying a memory stall and adding triple buffering cut kernel time by about 30% (125.5µs to 88µs).

insights.claim: Before this update, custom Pallas kernels appeared as single opaque blocks in XProf trace captures, giving developers no cycle-level visibility into their execution.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Identifies a real, previously unaddressed blind spot in TPU tooling for teams writing custom kernels, which matters as more AI workloads move to hand-tuned kernels for efficiency.
insights.locator: Before, these kernels appeared as single opaque blocks

insights.claim: According to Yogesh SY of Google's AI Infra team, the profiling gap comes from how profilers treat custom compilation paths: kernels made with Pallas, Mosaic, or Triton skip standard XLA passes, which can distort compile-time static cost models such that metrics like 'optimal FLOPs' and goodput efficiency may be inaccurate or not work at all.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: A specific, named root cause (custom kernels bypassing XLA passes) explaining why standard TPU efficiency metrics silently mislead teams using Pallas/Mosaic/Triton — actionable for any ML infra team currently trusting XLA-derived 'optimal FLOPs' numbers on custom kernels.
insights.locator: According to Yogesh SY of Google's AI Infra team

insights.claim: A static profiling tool can flag an MXU (matrix unit) instruction block as fully utilized while the unit actually sits idle waiting on HBM (high-bandwidth memory), because static analysis ignores time.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: A concrete illustration of why static cost models overstate hardware utilization on memory-bound kernels — a caution for anyone optimizing TPU kernels based on compile-time reports alone rather than runtime counters.
insights.locator: A static tool can flag an MXU instruction block

insights.claim: The suite works at three levels: compiler inspection via flags (--xla_enable_custom_call_region_trace=true and --xla_xprof_register_llo_debug_info=true) that surface lowered MLIR in a 'Custom Call Text' panel in the Graph Viewer; the Trace Viewer showing Low-Level Operations (LLO) bundle data including machine instructions per clock cycle across time-aligned tracks for the MXU, scalar/vector ALUs, vector fills, loads, spills, stores, and the cross-lane unit (XLU); and runtime hardware-counter sampling.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Gives engineers a concrete, reproducible workflow (specific flags and viewer panels) to diagnose whether custom kernel operations are fused and memory tiles structured as intended.
insights.locator: The suite works at three levels

insights.claim: For runtime telemetry, XProf samples hardware counters periodically with a 1µs resolution floor driven by a host-level timer, but a new external event-triggered mode removes that floor by capturing TPU trace instructions and boundary triggers (such as entry/exit of custom call scopes), enabling sub-microsecond capture and improved attribution.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Sub-microsecond event-triggered sampling is a meaningful precision upgrade for diagnosing fast-executing kernel operations that periodic 1µs sampling would previously miss or blur.
insights.locator: For runtime telemetry, XProf samples hardware counters

insights.claim: Developers can configure up to 28 counters per core across up to four SparseCores (a 4x28 matrix), collection is enabled through jax.profiler.ProfileOptions using tpu_enable_periodic_counter_sampling and tpu_tc_perf_counter_sampling_options with is_external_trigger:true, and periodic mode uses interval_us in place of the trigger flag.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: The hard 28-counters-per-core budget forces teams to prioritize which hardware signals to investigate per session rather than capturing everything at once — a real operational constraint for kernel-tuning workflows.
insights.locator: Developers can configure up to 28 counters per core

themes.theme: Case study and trust hierarchy for metrics

insights.claim: In a tiled matmul case study, a memory-bound variant showed large spikes in sync_wait counters; overlapping HBM loads with MXU compute through triple buffering reduced those sync_wait events and cut kernel time from 125.5µs to 88µs, roughly a 30% improvement, though the figure comes from a single Google-authored demo kernel rather than a broad benchmark, showing the workflow rather than gains to expect elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: The 30% figure is a workflow demonstration, not a generalizable benchmark — investors/engineers should not extrapolate this improvement rate to other kernels without their own profiling.
insights.locator: In the matmul case study, a memory-bound variant

insights.claim: Google's post sets out a 'hierarchy of trust' for metrics: values read directly from hardware registers (such as HBM utilization and TPO metrics) count as ground truth for custom kernels, while XLA cost-model estimates need caution; a new Perf Counters View lists over 16,000 raw counters in tabular form, and trace track height reflects the maximum raw counter value in an interval rather than a normalized percentage.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Establishes an explicit prioritization rule (hardware registers > XLA cost-model estimates) for interpreting TPU performance data — directly actionable guidance for any team optimizing Pallas/custom kernels.
insights.locator: The post also sets out a "hierarchy of trust"

insights.claim: The counter sampling capability is documented specifically for TPU v7 (Ironwood), so teams on earlier TPU generations should not assume the same coverage; the article recommends engineers stop treating XLA-derived efficiency numbers as reliable for custom kernels and instead anchor optimization on register-level counters.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: This feature is currently TPU v7-exclusive, a hardware-generation gating factor that matters for capacity/version planning by teams evaluating Google Cloud TPU infrastructure.
insights.locator: The counter sampling is documented for TPU v7
